items.notes:

Strongly recommended: Computer Science 8; Geography 12 (or W 12); any additional courses

sections.name: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR
sections.notes: Note: Geography 193, 198, 199, 199RA may be applied to any UD area by petition, depending on the subject matter, up to a maximum of 5 units. A maximum of 8 UD units from related fields may be applied to the major, if (a) they are selected from the approved list of related B.S. courses, or (b) are approved by petition. The list of related B.S. courses is available in the department office and on the department website.

narrative:
MAJOR REGULATIONSPREREQUISITES Check the General Catalog for the prerequisites to all listed courses.
P/NP GRADING OPTION Up to 5 units of the following courses may be taken P/NP for major credit: Geography 198, 199RA. All other major courses (prep or UD), including those applied to the major from other departments, must be completed on a letter-graded basis.
SUBSTITUTIONS In the major requirements are permissible only by petition to the department chair and dean.
G.P.A. REQUIREMENTS At least 2.0 overall UC average in all upper-division major courses and all courses (Prep and UD) for the major.
DOUBLE MAJORS With the approval of each department chairperson, up to a total of 8 units may be applied simultaneously to both UD majors.

nodes.title: Basic Astronomy
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.description: A survey of the development of astronomy with an emphasis on understanding the observable properties of the solar system, the sun and other stars, our own and other galaxies, and the entire universe. Topics of current interest will be discussed as time permits.

nodes.title: History of the Universe
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Astronomy 1.
nodes.description: Content will vary with the professor and student interests. Course has included modern extragalactic astronomy and cosmology, quasars, active galactic nuclei, dark matter, gravitational lenses, the early universe, the origins of life, and the possibility of extraterrestrial intelligence.

nodes.title: General Chemistry
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Statistics and Chemistry
nodes.description: Topics covered: atomic structure of matter; reaction stoichiometry; solution stoichiometry; gasses; quantum chemistry and the electronic structure of atoms; chemical bonding (molecular shapes, hybridization, and molecular orbital theory).

nodes.title: General Chemistry
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Statistics and Chemistry
nodes.prereq_text: CHEM 1A, CHEM 2A or CHEM 3A with a minimum grade of C-.
nodes.description: Topics covered: equilibrium; acids, bases, and buffers; thermochemistry (energy, enthalpy, entropy, and free energy); electrochemistry.

nodes.title: General Chemistry
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: CHEM 1B, CHEM 2B or CHEM 3B with a minimum grade of C-.
nodes.description: Topics covered: kinetics; intermolecular forces, liquids and solids; properties of solutions; transition metals and coordination complexes; organic chemistry and polymers; nuclear chemistry.

nodes.title: General Chemistry (Honors)
nodes.description: The sequence of topics will be similar to that in Chemistry 1A. Calculus will be used as needed, at the level of the concurrent Mathematics 3A course.

nodes.title: General Chemistry Lab (Part A)
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Statistics and Chemistry
nodes.prereq_text: CHEM 1A, CHEM 2A, or CHEM 3A with a minimum grade of C-. Concurrent enrollment, or a grade of C- or higher in CHEM 1B, CHEM 2B, or CHEM 3B.
nodes.description: Qualitative and quantitative measurements to develop laboratory techniques and demonstrate the basic concepts of stoichiometry, gas laws, atomic spectroscopy, chemical equilibrium, and acid-base chemistry.

nodes.title: General Chemistry (Honors)
nodes.prereq_text: CHEM 2A or CHEM 1A or CHEM 3A with a minimum grade of B.
nodes.description: Thermodynamics (first and second law), electrochemistry, chemical kinetics, atomic and molecular structure, and chemical bonding.

nodes.title: General Chemistry Laboratory (Part B)
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: CHEM 1B, CHEM 2B, or CHEM 3B with a minimum grade of C-. Concurrent enrollment, or a grade of C- or higher in CHEM 1C, CHEM 2C, or CHEM 3C. CHEM 2AL (may be taken concurrently).
nodes.description: Qualitative and quantitative measurements to develop laboratory techniques and demonstrate the basic concepts of buffers, thermochemistry, electrochemistry, kinetics, and colligative properties.

nodes.title: General Chemistry (Honors)
nodes.prereq_text: CHEM 2B or CHEM 1B or CHEM 3B with a minimum grade of B.
nodes.description: Structure and dynamics of the elements and their compounds. Aspects of technology and environmental problems.

nodes.title: General Chemistry (Majors)
nodes.prereq_text: None
nodes.description: Topics covered: atomic structure of matter; reaction stoichiometry; solution stoichiometry; gasses; quantum chemistry and the electronic structure of atoms; chemical bonding (molecular shapes, hybridization, and molecular orbital theory). First quarter of general chemistry intended for Chemistry Pre-Majors and Chemical Engineering Majors and others requiring a strong basis in chemistry.

nodes.title: General Chemistry (Majors)
nodes.prereq_text: CHEM 1A, CHEM 2A, or CHEM 3A with a minimum grade of C-.
nodes.description: Topics covered: equilibrium; acids, bases, and buffers; thermochemistry (energy, enthalpy, entropy, and free energy); electrochemistry. Second quarter of general chemistry intended for Chemistry Pre-Majors and Chemical Engineering Majors and others requiring a strong basis in chemistry.

nodes.title: General Chemistry (Majors)
nodes.prereq_text: CHEM 1B, CHEM 2B, or CHEM 3B with a minimum grade of C-.
nodes.description: Topics covered: kinetics; intermolecular forces, liquids and solids; properties of solutions; transition metals and coordination complexes; organic chemistry and polymers; nuclear chemistry. Third quarter of general chemistry intended for Chemistry Pre-Majors and Chemical Engineering Majors and others requiring a strong basis in chemistry.

nodes.title: Introduction to Computer Science
nodes.description: Introduction to computer program development for students with little to no programming experience. Basic programming concepts, variables and expressions, data and control structures, algorithms, debugging, program design, and documentation.

nodes.title: Statistical Analysis for Communication
nodes.description: An introduction to basic statistical concepts and applications in communication research. Through lecture and computer labs, students are exposed to the principles and procedures involved in quantitative data analysis.

nodes.title: Principles of Physical Geology
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.description: Introduction to the science of the Earth; properties and processes of its surface and interior, including plate tectonics, volcanism, earthquakes, glaciation, mountain building, formation of rocks, minerals, and the structural basis of landforms. Lab and lecture each offering. There can be an additional 1 day local field trip.

nodes.title: Principles of Historical Geology
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Earth 2 or 4 or 7 or 20.
nodes.description: Antiquity and history of the Earth from an Earth system history approach. Focus is on processes and changes over time of the Earth's lithosphere, biosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere.

nodes.title: Introduction to Oceanography
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.description: An introduction to oceanography covering the major physical, chemical, and geological features of the oceans, their role in Earth history, and potential use as a natural resource. Lab and lecture.

nodes.title: Dinosaurs
nodes.description: The origin and diversification of dinosaurs, including birds. Survey of evolutionary relationships within the group, and between the major groups of vertebrates. Broad introduction including anatomy, geography, climate, and vertebrate contemporaries.

nodes.title: Geological Catastrophes
nodes.description: Course deals with geologic catastrophes, e.g., earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis, and landslides. Students will learn the basic physical causes of these naturally occurring events and discuss the consequences.

nodes.title: Introduction to Geological and Geophysical Data Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: A. Statistical Analysis:
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A-B or 3A-B; and Mathematics 4A-B.
nodes.description: Various numerical methods for analysis of data are developed. Methods are statistical inference, error propagation, least squares, time series as applied to geological and geophysical examples. Lab and lecture.

nodes.title: Geological Applications of GIS
nodes.description: An intensive introduction to Geographic Information Systems (GIS) with an emphasis on geological applications, including geologic mapping, topographic analysis, modeling surface processes and river networks, importation and interpolation of field data, and spatial analysis and correlation of multiple geologic datasets. Short Lectures are interspersed with the lab exercises.

nodes.title: Principles of Soil Science
nodes.prereq_text: Environmental Studies 15A and 15B or Chemistry 1A-B; and Geography 3 or 4 or Earth Science 2 or 4 or 20
nodes.description: Explores core introductory concepts in soil science and how soils relate to global environmental challenges. Includes study of soil physical, biological, and chemical properties, soil development, and fertility, as well as the critical role of soils in fostering thriving communities. Incorporates independent projects and soils excursions.

nodes.title: Introductory Biology II--Ecology and Evolution
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: MCDB 1A with a grade of C- or better.
nodes.description: Introduction to population and community ecology, and evolution.

nodes.title: Introductory Biology Laboratory II
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Grade of C- or better in EEMB 2 (maybe taken concurrently).
nodes.description: Laboratory investigation s illustrate basis principles of ecology, evolution and biodiversity.

nodes.title: Introductory Biology III
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: MCDB 1A-B and EEMB 2 with a grade of C- or better.
nodes.description: Introduction to the major groups of microbes, plants, and animals.

groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives

nodes.title: Biometry
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: A. Statistical Analysis:
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A-B or 3A-B or 34A-B or 34LA-LB; and PSTAT 5A or PSTAT 5LS or PSTAT 109 or Math 4A or Psy 5; Completion of all listed prerequisites with a grade of C- or better.
nodes.description: Linear models and least squares fitting: simple and multiple linear regression; analysis of variance (fixed, random and mixed models; crossed and nested effects; balanced and unbalanced designs); analysis of covariance, factorial designs; incomplete layouts; use of transformations.

nodes.title: Introduction to Environmental Studies
nodes.description: Environmental Studies requires insights from many disciplines, including the social as well as biophysical science and the humanities. This introduction offers an overview of the field, examining both our planet and the ways in which we humans depend on it.

nodes.title: Introduction to Environmental Science
nodes.description: Provides integration of fundamental science with environmental topics. Includes impacts of human population increase; principles of systems and change, biogeochemical cycles, ecosystems and global climate; energy and laws of thermodynamics; water supply and pollution; toxicology and risk analysis; air pollution and stratospheric ozone depletion.

nodes.title: Introduction to the Social and Cultural Environment
nodes.description: An introduction to the relationship of societies and the environment from prehistorical times to the present. The course is global in perspective, and includes history, literature, philosophy, economics, science, and culture as evidence for examining the human social environment.

nodes.title: Environmental Chemistry 1
nodes.description: Introduction to chemistry from an environmental perspective. Introduces subatomic particles, nuclear instability and decay, radon, radiation, fission, fusion, nuclear power, half-life, nucleogenesis, cosmic abundance of elements, quantum mechanics, atomic orbitals, valence, the periodic chart, ionic and covalent bonding, moles, Earth layers, lithosphere, ores, mining, Iron Mountain Mine, acid mine drainage, and physical weathering. Weekly discussion section allows for review, questions, and quizzes.

nodes.title: Environmental Chemistry 2
nodes.prereq_text: Environmental Studies 15A.
nodes.description: A continuation of Environmental Chemistry 1. Explores the characteristics of water, solutions, chemical weathering, chemical reactions (redox, acid-base, precipitation, synthesis, decomposition, single displacement, double displacement), balancing chemical reactions, equilibrium, the hydrosphere and water cycle, issues of water chemistry, quality, and testing, sedimentation, fossil fuels and their combustion, an introduction to organic chemistry, common air pollutants, the chemistry of climate change.

nodes.title: Applied Ecology
nodes.description: Course provides an introduction to ecology: biological interactions and processes at the level of organisms, populations, communities and ecosystems. Ecological concepts are presented and discussed in the context of current challenges in environmental management and conservation.

nodes.title: Principles of Soil Science
nodes.prereq_text: Environmental Studies 15A and 15B or Chemistry 1A-B; and Geography 3 or 4 or Earth Science 2 or 4 or 20
nodes.description: Explores core introductory concepts in soil science and how soils relate to global environmental challenges. Includes study of soil physical, biological, and chemical properties, soil development, and fertility, as well as the critical role of soils in fostering thriving communities. Incorporates independent projects and soils excursions.

nodes.title: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) for Environmental Applications
nodes.prereq_text: Environmental Studies 2 or Geography 4 or Earth Sciences 2; and either Environmental Studies 1 or 3.
nodes.description: Explores how Geographic Information Systems (GIS) can help environmental researchers and professionals analyze and communicate the spatial patterns underpinning a wide variety of environmental concerns. Introduces students to the basic theory and application of GIS through hands-on application of the technology to environmental questions.

nodes.title: Oceans and Atmosphere
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Geography and Mathematics
nodes.description: Introduction to the oceans and atmosphere and their role in the Earth's climate and its weather patterns. Focus on the flows of solar energy through the ocean and atmosphere systems. Human impacts of the Earth's climate are also introduced.

nodes.title: Land, Water and Life
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Geography and Mathematics
nodes.description: Study of the interactions among water, landforms, soil, and vegetation that create and modify the surface of the Earth. Impacts of physical environment on human societies and humans as agents of environmental change.

nodes.title: People, Place, and Environment
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Geography and Mathematics
nodes.description: Survey of spatial differentiation and organization of human activity and interaction with the Earth's biophysical systems. Sample topics include human spatial decision-making behavior, migration, population growth, economic development, industrial location, urbanization, and human impacts on the natural environment.

nodes.title: Introduction to Global Warming
nodes.description: Overview of global warming and climate change processes. Description of complex relationships between scientific, technological, economic, social, political, and historical facets of global warming and climate change. Introduction to the concept and practice of climate modeling.

nodes.title: Maps and Spatial Reasoning
nodes.description: Surveys properties of maps, emphasizing map use and interpretation. Lecture topics include map abstraction, generalization, map projections, and symbolization. Special purpose maps, thematic maps, and the display of quantitative and qualitative information is considered.

nodes.title: Introduction to Programming in Geographical Sciences
nodes.description: Introduction to computer programming for students with little to no programming experience. Covers basic programming concepts, variables and expressions, data and control structures, algorithms, debugging and programming design. Additionally, the course covers object-oriented programming, libraries and modules. Emphasis is on hands-on experience and exercises using Python as the programming language.

nodes.title: Introduction to Environmental Optics in Physical Geography
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: B. Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3A or 3 and 3B or 4, and 115A.
nodes.description: Basic physical principles of electromagnetic radiation in the environment and their application to physical geography and remote sensing. Radiative transfer in the atmosphere, oceans, snow and ice, inland waters, rock, soil, and vegetation. Spectral signatures in remote sensing.

nodes.title: Physical Geography of the World's Oceans
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: B. Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Introduction to the processes which control the circulation of the world's oceans. Topics include: wind driven circulation, thermohaline circulation, water masses, waves, and tides.

nodes.title: Urban Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 5.
nodes.description: Introduction to the study of the economic geography of cities and regions and its relation to planning: urbanization, internal structure of cities, settlement systems, regional growth and development, migration, transportation, housing.

nodes.title: Economic Geography
nodes.prereq_text: upper-division standing only
nodes.description: Introduction to the study of spatial economic theories with applications at the urban, regional, and global scales. Topics include settlement system dynamics and regional development, land economics and land use policies, and regional inequality and poverty.

nodes.title: Introduction to Meteorology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: B. Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: GEOG 3 or 3A or ENVS 3 or EARTH 2 or 4; and Math 2A-B or 3A-B; and PHYS 1 or 6A; and upper division standing
nodes.description: An introduction to the dynamics of the earth's atmosphere. Topics include: energy exchange mechanisms, energy balance, condensation and precipitation processes, the dynamics of pressure and wind systems, and the distributions of weather disturbances.

nodes.title: Environmental Hydrology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: B. Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Analysis of the water cycle with emphasis on land-atmosphere interactions, precipitation-runoff, flood, snow melt, and infiltration processes.

groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography

nodes.title: Principles of Soil Science
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: B. Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Environmental Studies 15A and 15B or Chemistry 1A-B; and Geography 3 or 4 or Earth Science 2 or 4 or 20
nodes.description: Explores core introductory concepts in soil science and how soils relate to global environmental challenges. Includes study of soil physical, biological, and chemical properties, soil development, and fertility, as well as the critical role of soils in fostering thriving communities. Incorporates independent projects and soils excursions.

nodes.title: Soils of California: Formation, Morphology, and Management
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Environmental Studies 114A or Geography 114A or Earth Science 184A with a grade C or higher.
nodes.description: Course dives into soil genesis, classification, and sustainable land use in the context of California’s diverse soils. Connects soil characteristics and landscapes to communities, conservation, ecological relationships, agriculture, and climate change. Covers field safety, soil descriptions, and field methods via hands-on field experiences during lab.

nodes.title: Remote Sensing of the Environment 1
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Introduction to theory and methods of aerial photography and satellite remote sensing for studying Earths environment, from natural vegetation to urban areas. Lab develops fundamental skills in the acquisition, interpretation, and analysis of digital remote sensing imagery.

nodes.title: Remote Sensing of the Environment 2
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 115A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Properties of satellite imagery and tools required to process data from remote sensing systems. Topics include spectral and spatial enhancement, image classification, geometric and radiometric correction, with emphasis on applications. Lab includes analysis of optical, thermal, Lidar, and radar data.

nodes.title: Remote Sensing of the Environment 3
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 115B with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Advanced image processing, including data fusion and resampling techniques, atmospheric corrections, global navigation satellite systems, and hyperspatial sensors with emphasis on applications. Lab is centered around projects (e.g., glacial and vegetation changes in mountain environments) with poster presentation of results.

nodes.title: Groundwater Hydrology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: GEOG 3B or 4 or EARTH 2; or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Analysis of groundwater flow in complex geologic environments, aquifer properties, wells and groundwater contamination, surface water-groundwater interactions. Laboratory: basic groundwater experiments, Darcy's law, flow nets, solute dispersion, field measurements of bedrock groundwater, analysis of pumping-test data.

nodes.title: Scientific Research Methods in Geography
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 5; and, Geography 3 or 3A or 3B or 4.
nodes.description: Introduction to scientific research methods in human, physical, and techniques geography. Topics include: scientific logic and philosophy, physical measurement, surveys, experimental and nonexperimental research designs, computational modeling, sampling, data analysis and display, written and oral communication, and research ethics.

nodes.title: Climatic Change and Its Consequences
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A or Geography 8 or Earth Science 2 or Earth Science 3 or Earth Science 4 or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Mechanisms and processes which produce climate change. Methods for reconstructing paleo-climates. Impacts of past climate change on human societies.

groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques

nodes.title: The Urban Environment
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3B or 4 or Environmental Studies 2 or permission of the instructor.
nodes.description: Environment and climate of cities, suburbs, and other settlements, focusing on the built environment, soils, water, solar radiation, atmosphere, vegetation, and human thermal comfort. Lab includes field work on a range of sites along an urban-to-exurban gradient, individual lab reports on specific urban sites, use of a web wiki to produce collaborative data, and a final synthesis assignment.

nodes.title: Mountain Weather and Climate
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: B. Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A or 3B or 4; or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Overview of orographic weather patterns with focus on orographic precipitation and circulation, mountain waves, cloudiness, snowfall and avalanches, fire weather, air pollution and dispersion. Human impacts on mountain environments and climate change in mountain areas are introduced.

nodes.title: Coastal Pollution
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: GEOG 3A
nodes.description: A survey of the source and fate of pollutants in the coastal ocean, focusing specifically on the physical processes that govern the transport of nutrients, sediment, hydrocarbons, and human pathogens in coastal ecosystems. Material includes readings from scientific papers, grey literature, and news media in order to develop intuition for how transport phenomena frame both pollution issues and solutions.

nodes.title: Tropical Meteorology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: MATH 2A or 3A with grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Description of tropical atmosphere. High and low frequency variability: hurricanes, monsoon, El Nino, satellite observations, and modeling.

nodes.title: Earth System Science
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: B. Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A or 3B or 4 or equivalent course.
nodes.description: Description of various components of earth system: climate and hydrologic systems, biogeochemical dynamics, ecological dynamics, human interactions, and global change. Observations and modeling of earth system.

nodes.title: FIELD STUDIES IN WATER, ENERGY, AND ECOSYSTEMS
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: GEOG 3B or equivalent, plus one or more upper division course(s) in the area(s) of atmospheric science, hydrology, ecology, or geological science.
nodes.description: Introduction to the principles of environmental observation and the application of environmental physics to understanding the spatial and temporal dynamics of water and energy flows within local Californian ecosystems. Field work completed during break between winter and spring quarters.

nodes.title: Quantitative Geomorphology
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3B or 4; or Earth 2
nodes.description: Basic quantitative understanding of processes shaping Earth's surface. In-depth evaluation of hill slope diffusion, mass wasting, and fluvial processes. Applications of quantitative methods are emphasized throughout class. Laboratory provides understanding of isotopic, physical, and remote sensing data.

nodes.title: Environmental Impacts in Human History
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing; or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Interactions between human history and the environment are explored. Example topics include early Earth history, long term climate change, the origin of agriculture, short term climate change, the origin of importance of disease and invasive species.

nodes.title: Global Biogeochemical Cycles
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A or 3B or 4; or, Environmental Studies 2; or, Earth Science 1; or, Chemistry 1A.
nodes.description: Examines processes driving element and energy cycling through the Earth system. Aim is to understand global patterns of element fluxes, dynamic nature of element/energy cycles, and prediction of biogeochemical cycling with changes in climate and human impacts.

nodes.title: Form, Process, and Human Use of Rivers
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A-2B or 3A-3B or 34A-B.
nodes.description: Basic understanding of fluvial (river) hydrology. In-depth evaluation of channel form and fluvial processes and impact of human use on rivers.

groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography

nodes.title: The California Channel Islands
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
nodes.prereq_text: MCDB 1A-1AL and EEMB 2; or MCDB 20 or EEMB 22 or Environmental Studies 2 or 60 or Geography 3 or 3A or 3B or 4 orEarth Science 2.
nodes.description: Discussion of biological, geological, ecological, anthropological, and oceanographic characteristics of the Channel Islands area as well as the management and human uses of this region. Emphasis on islands and ocean waters off Southern California.

nodes.title: Geography of the United States
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Not open to freshman.
nodes.description: Intensive study of the physical and cultural processes that have shaped and are shaping the landscapes of the United States.

nodes.title: Geography of Latin America
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 5 or Global Studies 1 or 2 or Environmental Studies 1 or 2 or 3.
nodes.description: El Pueblo, a vila, li tenamit: however you call where you live, geography matters. How and why are human and physical patterns inscribed where they are on the Latin American landscape?

nodes.title: Introduction to Marine Resources
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A and Geography 3B or 4.
nodes.description: Introduction to the marine resources of the California coast. The interplay of oceanographic, climatic, biogeochemical and geologic factors and the influences of humankind will be addressed. Topics include: climate, circulation, biogeography, fisheries, marine mammals, petroleum, pollution and exploration history.

groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography

nodes.title: Food, Agriculture, and the Environment
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Our global food system is in crisis. Responsible for approximately a third of global greenhouse gas emissions, it leaves over a quarter of the worlds people suffering from moderate or severe food insecurity. Yet the food system also holds some of the most promising opportunities for just transition to a more sustainable and equitable society. This survey course introduces the history and structure of the global food system, pressing current challenges, and exciting potential solutions.

nodes.title: Environmental Water Quality
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Upper-division standing.
nodes.description: Study of physio-chemical and biological characteristics of natural waters, analysis of water pollution and treatment, water-quality regulations. Laboratory: independent and supervised research on water pollutants and treatment, quantitative analysis of water-quality data and one-day field work.

nodes.title: Ocean Circulation
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A or Earth Science 4.
nodes.description: Examination of the general circulation of the oceans and its impact on global climate and climate change. Topics include properties of seawater, forces driving ocean currents, wind and buoyancy generation of basin scale circulations, and their impact on global climate.

groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography

nodes.title: Ocean Carbon Cycle and Climate
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Chemistry 1A; and Geography 3 or 104 or Earth Science 4
nodes.description: Examination of the ocean carbon cycle and its influence on Earth's climate and climate change. Topics include carbonate system chemistry, photosynthesis and respiration, anthropogenic carbon, and climate change. Current research in carbon cycle and climate is also discussed.

nodes.title: Biogeography: The Study of Plant and Animal Distributions
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: B. Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A or 3B or 4 or Environmental Studies 2 or EEMB 2 or Earth Science 2.
nodes.description: Basic processes governing geographic distribution patterns of biota, including migration, evolution, isolation, and endemism. Biogeographic regions and their histories and an introduction to island biogeography. Emphasis on plants and plant geography. One all-day field trip.

groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography

nodes.title: Intermediate Geographical Data Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: A. Statistical Analysis:
nodes.prereq_text: Statistics and Applied Probability 5AA-ZZ or Ecology, Evolution & Marine Biology 30 or Psychology 5 or Communication 87.

items.text: Statistics and Applied Probability 5AA-ZZ or Ecology

nodes.description: Quantitative methods for the analysis of geographical data. Topics include spatial clustering, spatial auto-correlation, spatial regression, and introductory methods for analyzing point, area (lattice), and continuous data. Lab includes the use of statistical software for exploratory spatial data analysis.

nodes.title: Measuring our Environment
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A and 3B or 4.
nodes.description: Introduction to measurement and interpretation of physical-environmental data (temperature, humidity, precipitation) and integrated environmental measures (e.g. potential evapotranspiration). Working with micrometeorological towers deployed across an environmental gradient, students develop and test hypothesis using real-time tower data.

nodes.title: Introduction to Geographic Information Systems and Science
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Upper Division Unit Standing
nodes.description: Comprehensive overview of Geographic Information Systems and Science. Topics span the nature of geographic information and the procedures for operating GIS. Labs provide hands-on experience with GIS and related software.

nodes.title: Technical Issues in Geographic Information Systems
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: A minimum grade of C in Geography 176A.
nodes.description: Study of the technical issues underlying geographic information systems, including coordinate systems and analytic geometry, database models and structures, algorithms and analytical procedures. Laboratory analysis of digital geographic information from physical and social sources.

nodes.title: GIS Design and Applications
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 176B with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Applying GIS theory and techniques to solve problems in land and resource management, utilities, and municipal government. Covers all stages of a GIS project: planning, design, analysis, and presentation. Students collaborate to design, develop, and present a GIS pilot study.

groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques

nodes.title: ANALYSIS AND MODELING OF MOVEMENT
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 176A or Geography 12/W12 or Environmental Studies 154 or Earth Science 176; and, Computer Science 8 or Geography 13; or equivalent course work; or consent of instructor
nodes.description: Many geographic, social, and natural systems involve dynamic processes or movement of individuals in space and time. Examples include animal migration, human mobility, disease diffusion, and natural disasters like hurricanes and wildfires. Movement is key to understanding these dynamic processes. This course reviews computational methods for analysis, modeling and simulation of movement in ecological and human systems. Students gain an understanding of spatiotemporal processes and patterns, and develop computational skills to process trajectory data, analyze movement patterns, and apply movement models.

nodes.title: Close-Range Remote Sensing of Earth Surface Processes
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: GEOG 3 or 4, Upper Division unit standing
nodes.description: Introduction to close-range remote sensing for interpreting and detecting changes in Earth surface processes and landscapes. Topics include: unpiloted aerial systems (UAS), LIDAR (aerial, terrestrial), autonomous camera systems, Structure-from-Motion photogrammetry, spatial-temporal change detection, etc. Review key principles, methods, and technologies of both active (e.g., laser-based) and passive (e.g., photogrammetric based) sensors. Experiential learning via interactive lectures and hands-on, field-based lab assignments.

nodes.title: Location Theory and Modeling
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: MATH 2A or 3A or 34A or consent of instructor.
nodes.description: A technical overview of location analysis and modeling in the context of GIScience. Applications associated with emergency service planning, natural resource management, retail site selection, among others, will be relied upon to make connections among models, spatial information and interpretation of findings. Utilization and implementation considerations using GIS and commercial optimization software will be explored.

nodes.title: Introduction to Optimization Methods for Geographic Problems
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: D. Geographical Techniques
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A, 3A, or 34A.
nodes.description: Introduction to spatial optimization methods that are used in the analysis of geographic problems, including linear programming, network programming, integer programming, and dynamic programming. Example problems involving spatial temporal decision making are emphasized. Lab section includes the use of optimization software for analysis, planning and decision making.

nodes.title: Urban and Environmental System Analysis
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Geography 3 or 3A or 3B or 4 or 5 or 108 or 109.
nodes.description: Applications of operations research techniques and decision analysis in structuring approaches to urban and environmental problems. Examples are drawn from problems in facility location, regional models, transportation and other networks, utility corridors and similar problems.

nodes.title: Field Study of California's Coast
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: E. Integrative and Regional Geography
nodes.prereq_text: Consent of instructor.
nodes.description: Explores the physical geography of California's southern and central coast by way of field trips to iconic and interesting beaches, estuaries, bluffs, dunes, and salt marshes combined with topical lectures and guest speakers. Field trips may involve visiting parks, restored ecosystems, government facilities, or urban areas. Issues of landscape management and human-environment interactions in the coastal zone will also be explored. Student projects will study a visited site, or one of their own interest, and investigate its environmental and human histories, modern dynamics, and/or future challenges.

nodes.title: Coastal Landscapes and Processes
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: C. Specialized Physical Geography
nodes.prereq_text: GEOG 3 or 4 or EARTH 1 or 2
nodes.description: Introduction to coastal landscapes and their formative processes, including: beaches, dunes, barriers, bluffs, estuaries, salt marshes, nearshore bars, marine terraces, etc. Overview of key theories, concepts, models, and research in coastal geomorphology. Applications for understanding real-world issues such as sea-level rise, coastal erosion and flooding, land use planning, and ecosystem restoration will also be explored. Experiential learning via interactive lectures, local field trips, hands-on learning of field methods, and an independent project based on student interests.

nodes.title: Maps and Spatial Reasoning
nodes.description: Surveys properties of maps, emphasizing map use and interpretation. Lecture topics include map abstraction, generalization, map projections, and symbolization. Special purpose maps, thematic maps, and the display of quantitative and qualitative information is considered.

nodes.title: Global History, Culture and Ideology
nodes.description: A survey of the historical processes that have brought different areas of the world into closer contact. Topics include ideologies of nationalism, democracy, and liberalism; international trade and migrations; technological changes; colonialism; the globalization of culture; and the reactions to them.

nodes.title: Global Socioeconomic and Political Processes
nodes.description: Examination of contemporary social, economic, political, and environmental change in a global context; the emergence of a global economy and new systems of world order; and the debate over globalization and whether or not it is desireable.

nodes.title: Calculus with Algebra and Trigonometry
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Geography and Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Qualifying score on the Mathematics Placement Exam.

requires.text: Qualifying score on the Mathematics Placement Exam

nodes.description: Math 3A with precalculus: A function approach integrating algebra, trigonometry, and differential calculus. Topics include: one-on-one and onto functions; inverse functions; properties and graphs of polynomial, rational, exponential, and logarithmic functions; properties and graphs of trigonometric functions; analytic geometry; functions and limits; derivatives; techniques and applications of differentiation; introduction to integration; logarithmic and trigonometric functions.

nodes.title: Calculus with Algebra and Trigonometry
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Geography and Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Math 3B with precalculus: A continued review of relevant topics from precalculus (see Math 2A); integral calculus, including definite and indefinite integrals; techniques of integration, introduction to sequences and series; with applications in mathematics and physics.

nodes.title: Calculus with Applications, First Course
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Geography and Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Qualifying score on the Mathematics Placement Exam.

requires.text: Qualifying score on the Mathematics Placement Exam

nodes.description: Differential Calculus including analytic geometry, functions and limits, derivatives, techniques and applications of differentiation; introduction to integration; logarithmic and trigonometric functions.

nodes.title: Calculus with Applications, Second Course
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Geography and Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 3A with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Integral calculus including definite and indefinite integrals, techniques of integration; introduction to sequences and series; with applications in mathematics and physics.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra with Applications
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Geography and Mathematics
nodes.prereq_text: Math 2B or 3B or 3BI with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Systems of linear equations, matrix algebra, determinants, vector spaces and subspaces, basis and dimension, linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalization, and orthogonality.

nodes.title: Differential Equations
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Math 4A or Math 4AI with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: First and second order differential equations, separation of variables, linear differential equations, systems of first order equations, nonlinear differential equations and stability.

nodes.title: Vector Calculus with Applications, First Course
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4A (or 4AI) with a letter grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Calculus of functions of several variables, vector valued functions of one variable, derivative and integrals of vector functions, double and triple integrals, properties and applications of integrals, change of variables.

nodes.title: Vector calculus with Applications, Second Course
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4B (or 4BI) and Mathematics 6A, each with a minimum grade of C.
nodes.description: Scalar and vector fields, integration along paths, integration over surfaces and solid regions, integral theorems of vector calculus, Fourier series, partial differential equations.

nodes.title: Transition to Higher Mathematics
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 4A or 4AI or 4B or 4BI or 6A or 6B with a grade of B or better.
nodes.description: Introduction to the elements of propositional logic, techniques of mathematical proof, and fundamental mathematical structures, including sets, functions, relations, and other topics as time permits. Mastery of this material is essential for students planning to major in mathematics.

nodes.title: Calculus for Social and Life Sciences
nodes.description: Introduction to differential and integral calculus with applications to modeling in the biological sciences.

nodes.title: Calculus for Social and Life Sciences
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A or 3A or 34A or 34LA with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Continued study of differential and integral calculus with differential andintegral calculus with applications. Introduction to mathematical modeling with differential equations. Calculus of several variables including an introduction to partial derivatives.

nodes.title: Calculus for the Life Sciences
nodes.description: Applications of differential and integral calculus to the life sciences. Includes mathematical foundations, biology examples, and computer programming to simulate dynamic systems.

nodes.title: Calculus for the Life Sciences
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A or 3A or 34A or 34LA with a grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Applications of differential and integral calculus to the life sciences. Includes mathematical foundations, biology examples, and computer programming to simulate dynamic systems of more than one equation.

groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Chemistry 1A-B-C with a grade of C- or better (Chem 1C may be taken concurrently), or a score of 4 or better on either the Advanced Placement Chemistry or Advanced Placement Biology exams.

items.text: a score of 4 or better on either the Advanced Placement Chemistry or Advanced Placement Biology exams

groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives

groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Lower-Division Electives
nodes.prereq_text: Grade of C- or better in MCDB 1A (may be taken concurrently).
nodes.description: Laboratory investigations illustrate basic principles of biochemistry, molecular and cell biology, development, genetics & physiology.

nodes.title: Concepts of Biology
nodes.description: Introduction to the science of life; cells, genetics, metabolism, molecular biology, physiology, natural selection, evolution, ecosystems; current news and controversial topics in biology.

nodes.title: Basic Physics
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Basic Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A or 3A or AP Math AB Exam with a score of 3 or better.

items.text: AP Math AB Exam with a score of 3 or better

nodes.description: Introduction to classical mechanics for students in engineering and the physical sciences. Measurement, units, and foundations of physics; vectors; kinematics; circular motion; forces, mass, and Newton's laws; center of mass; momentum; work and energy; conservation laws; collisions; rotational kinematics.

nodes.title: Basic Physics
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Basic Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Physics 1 with a grade of C- or better; Mathematics 2A-B or 3A-B or AP Math BC exam with a score of 3 or better.

nodes.description: Rotational dynamics and angular momentum; equilibrium and elasticity; periodic motion including LRC electrical circuits; gravitation; fluid mechanics; temperature; thermal expansion; heat and the first law of thermodynamics; heat conduction; kinetic theory of gases; entropy and the second law; heat engines.

groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Basic Physics

items.text: AP Math BC Exam score of 3 or better

nodes.description: Mechanical waves, wave interference and normal modes, sound and hearing, electric field, Gauss's law, electric potential, capacitance and dielectrics, current, resistance, electromotive force, DC circuits.

nodes.prereq_text: Physics 3 or 23 (may be taken concurrently).

nodes.prereq_text: Physics 3 with a grade of C- or better.
nodes.description: Magnetic fields, electromagnetic induction and inductance, AC circuits, Maxwell's equations, electromagnetic waves, light and geometrical optics, interference and diffraction.

nodes.title: Physics Laboratory
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Basic Physics

nodes.description: Introductory laboratory emphasizing magnetism, circuits and optics.

nodes.title: Introductory Physics

nodes.description: Presents concepts and methodologies for understanding physical phenomena, and is particularly useful preparation for upper-division study in the life sciences. Vectors, velocity, acceleration. Newton's laws. Work and energy. Linear momentum. Gravity. Static equilibrium. Rotational motion. Angular momentum.

nodes.title: Introductory Physics
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Physics 6 Series
nodes.prereq_text: Physics 6A with a minimum grade of C-.
nodes.description: Presents concepts and methodologies for understanding physical phenomena, and is particularly useful preparation for upper-division study in the life sciences. Oscillatory motion. Vibrations, waves, sound. Fluids. Electrostatics and DC circuits. Magnetism and magnetic forces. Induction and Faraday's law. AC circuits. If time permits: Heat and thermodynamics.

nodes.title: Introductory Physics
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Physics 6 Series
nodes.prereq_text: Physics 6B with a minimum grade of C-.
nodes.description: Presents concepts and methodologies for understanding physical phenomena, and is particularly useful preparation for upper-division study in the life sciences. Electromagnetic waves. Geometric optics, optical instruments. Interference and diffraction. Quantum theory of the atom. Nuclear physics. If time permits: Special relativity, elementary particle physics.

nodes.title: Physics Laboratory
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Physics 7 Series
nodes.prereq_text: Physics 7B; Co-requisite: Physics 7C
nodes.description: Periodic motion, sound, and basic electronics, while emphasizing good laboratory techniques such as uncertainty propagation, statistical analysis, developing and testing models, and good report writing.

nodes.title: Introduction to Mathematical Methods for Physics
nodes.description: Single variable functions, derivatives and integrals with applications to kinematics. Taylor series. Introduction to ordinary differential equations and Newtons second law as an ODE. Vectors and scalars with physics applications. Dot and cross products. Matrices and determinants. Unit circle and trigonometric identities. Polar coordinates and kinematics in polar coordinates.

nodes.title: General Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Mathematics 2A/3A and Mathematics 2B/3B or Physics 8 or AP Calculus BC Exam score of 5.
nodes.description: Classical mechanics, kinematics, vectors, Newtons laws, work and energy, conservation laws, rotational kinematics.

nodes.title: General Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Physics 21 with a grade of C- or better.
nodes.description: Rotational dynamics, fluid mechanics, gravitation, periodic motion, temperature and heat, thermodynamics.

nodes.title: General Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Physics 22 with a minimum grade of C- or better.
nodes.description: Mechanical waves, sound, electric charge and electric field, Gauss Law, electric potential, capacitance and dielectrics, current, resistance, electromotive force, DC circuits.

nodes.title: General Physics
nodes.prereq_text: Physics 23 with a minimum grade of C-; Mathematics 4A.
nodes.description: Magnetic fields, electromagnetic induction and inductance, AC circuits, Maxwell's equations, electromagnetic waves, light and geometrical optics, interference and diffraction.

nodes.title: Understanding Data
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Statistics and Chemistry
nodes.description: Introduction to data science. Concepts of statistical thinking. Topics include random variables, sampling distributions, hypothesis testing, correlation and regression. Visualizing, analyzing and interpreting real world data using Python. Computing labs required.

nodes.title: Statistics for Life Sciences
groups: PREPARATION FOR THE MAJOR: Statistics and Chemistry
nodes.description: An introduction to statistics for students interested in the quantitative analysis of problems in the life sciences. The focus is on application; topics include probability, correlation and regression, sampling distributions, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: A. Statistical Analysis:
nodes.prereq_text: Math 3C or Math 4A or Math 4AI or Math 6A or Math 6AI completed with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Concepts of probability; random variables; combinatorial probability; discrete and continuous distributions; joint distributions, expected values; moment generating functions; law of large numbers and central limit theorems.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
groups: UPPER-DIVISION MAJOR: A. Statistical Analysis:
nodes.prereq_text: Math 3C or Math 4A or Math 4AI or Math 6A or Math 6AI completed with a minimum grade of C or better.
nodes.description: Concepts of probability; random variables; combinatorial probability; discrete and continuous distributions; joint distributions, expected values; moment generating functions; law of large numbers and central limit theorems.
